source: Cross (1982; reprinted 2024) Designerly ways of knowing, Design Studies 3(4):221-227
finding: Cross argues design is a third area of general education beside sciences and humanities. Its value comes from deep patterns of how designers think and act, called designerly ways of knowing. He proposes this as an axiomatic touch-stone theory for design as a discipline.
numbers: No experiment. Paper is 7 pages (221-227). Reference list read: Lawson 1979, Darke 1979, Rittel and Webber 1973, Simon 1969, Ferguson 1977, Hillier and Leaman 1974, Cross, Naughton and Walker 1981.
limits: Only the abstract page and reference list were readable (paywall). The five-aspect list in the next line is from memory.
agent_relevance: Defines the object of study as a way of knowing, not a method. Our schema could treat design moves as a distinct operator family.
quote: there are designerly ways of knowing

source: Cross (1982) five aspects of designerly knowing (as recalled)
finding: Recalled, not verified this session: designers tackle ill-defined problems; the mode is solution-focused; thinking is constructive; designers use codes that translate abstract requirements into concrete objects; designers use non-verbal media such as sketches and models.
numbers: none
limits: Unverified. Check against the full paper before use.
agent_relevance: Candidate operator list: solution conjecture first, code translation, sketch externalisation.

source: Cross (2024 ch.1 reprint) reference list: Lawson 1979 Cognitive strategies in architectural design, Ergonomics 22(1):59-68
finding: Lawson 1979 is the empirical base Cross 1982 cites for the claim that designers work solution-first.
numbers: Citation only: Ergonomics 22(1), pp. 59-68. Cross 1982 also cites Lawson 1980 book How Designers Think.
limits: Citation seen; paper text not opened. Sample sizes and scores not verified.
agent_relevance: Founding experiment to replicate with LLMs: block-arrangement puzzle, problem-focused vs solution-focused strategy.

source: Lawson (1979) architects vs science students on a coloured-block puzzle (as recalled)
finding: Recalled: final-year architecture students and postgraduate science students arranged coloured blocks to meet hidden rules. Scientists tended to explore the problem to find the rule. Architects tended to propose solutions and learn the rules from the feedback.
numbers: Group sizes and scores not verified.
limits: Unverified from memory. Wikipedia (opened) confirms only the direction of the finding.
agent_relevance: Test an LLM on a hidden-rule puzzle: does it probe the rule, or propose arrangements and learn from rejections?

source: Wikipedia: Design thinking (section Solution-focused thinking)
finding: States that in empirical studies of three-dimensional problem solving Lawson found architects used solution-focused strategies, distinct from the problem-focused strategies of scientists. Quotes Cross: designers use solution conjectures to develop understanding of the problem.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary source. Gives no sample sizes.
agent_relevance: Supports a solution-conjecture-first operator. Pair with G3: a conjecture must be tested on output the answer was not fitted to.
quote: Designers tend to use solution conjectures as the means of developing their understanding of the problem

source: Wikipedia: Design thinking (history and wicked problems)
finding: Lawson's 1980 book began generalising design thinking. Cross 1982 set out intrinsic qualities of design thinking for general education. Rowe 1987 Design Thinking described architects' methods. Rittel and Webber contrasted wicked problems with tame ones; wicked problems have no definitive formulation, no true/false solution, and wide disagreement on the situation. David Kelley founded IDEO in 1991.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary. Tame/wicked is a contrast, not a measured variable.
agent_relevance: Wicked problems have no stop test. Our guardrails need a different stop rule when no check exists.

source: Wikipedia: Nigel Cross
finding: Cross began with Wizard-of-Oz computer-aided-design studies in the 1960s, helped start the Design Thinking Research Symposia in 1991 with Delft, and with Dorst advanced co-evolution of problem space and solution space. Books: Designerly Ways of Knowing (2006, 2nd ed 2025), Design Thinking (2011, 2nd ed 2023).
numbers: DTRS series started 1991; DTRS2 at Delft in 1994 laid foundations for protocol studies.
limits: Biographical. No effect sizes.
agent_relevance: The 1994 DTRS protocol data set is the shared corpus behind many co-evolution results.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution, Design Studies 22(5)
finding: Recalled: protocol study of experienced industrial designers on a design brief. Creative moments came when a bridge formed between problem and solution frames, and both spaces were refined together.
numbers: Recalled N about 9 designers, about 2.5 hours each. Not verified.
limits: Unverified. Cited in 2503.01631 (opened) as showing designers seek extra information when stuck and that frame shifts bring creative insight.
agent_relevance: Argues against a strict define-then-solve pipeline. Allow problem restatement in the loop after a failed check (G1, G2).

source: Shin et al. (2025, CHI) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing
finding: Large crowd study. Using GPT-4o in three ways (free-form, direct generation, structured by Dorst's reframing steps) did not raise novelty or usefulness of problem frames compared with no LLM.
numbers: 456 recruited, 280 kept; 15 expert raters; pilot N=36; three problems; all LLM-vs-manual comparisons p>0.05; sample sized for 95% power at medium effect (needed 220 and 280).
limits: Crowd workers, one model, one session, standardised prompts with buttons. Time on task: manual 23.25 min, direct 21.82, structured 28.35, free-form 20.78.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the model can reframe. Reframing needs a check; the schema's reframe operator should fire only on a signal (G1).
quote: using LLMs does not help improve the quality of problem frames

source: Shin et al. (2025) expertise gap
finding: LLM use widened the gap between experienced and inexperienced reframers. Experts made more novel frames and felt more agency than novices.
numbers: Experts (3+ correct of 5 quiz items) made 12.54% more novel frames than novices under LLM conditions (t=2.70, p=0.01); free-form gap 20.84% (p=0.06, not significant); structured agency gap 15.69% (p=0.02); usefulness no difference.
limits: Expert/novice split by a 5-item quiz, a coarse proxy.
agent_relevance: The value of LLM output depends on a judge who can pick good frames. Our code-checked selection (G5) stands in for that judge.

source: Shin et al. (2025) why LLM frames did not help
finding: 93 of 218 LLM-group participants reported problems. Reasons: LLM ideas were not novel (n=31), repetitive (n=14), not useful (n=12). One participant said the model could not grasp the why of human behaviour.
numbers: 93 of 218; n=31, 14, 12. Only 12 voiced loss-of-agency concerns. Structured approach gave no higher helpfulness than others (H3 rejected).
limits: Self-report reasons. Prompt tuning: GPT-4o needed a short definition of paradoxical problems and a length cap; step order for steps 8-9 was reversed from Dorst.
agent_relevance: Reframing prompts need explicit definitions and length limits. Reordered steps (assess themes, then frame) suited the model better than the human order.

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024, CHI) Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking
finding: Between-participants sketching task (chatbot avatar) after seeing an example design. Midjourney support raised fixation on the example, and gave fewer ideas with less variety and lower originality than no support.
numbers: N=60 (three conditions: no support, Google Image Search, Midjourney). Fixation: GenAI mean .32, 89% CI [.11,.55], Bayes factor 124; image search .27 [.05,.49], BF 42.48. Originality total effect GenAI -.03 [-.06,.00], BF 35. Fluency GenAI total effect negative, BF 3.20; variety -.29 [-.75,.16], BF 5.93.
limits: Image model, not a text LLM; one task; Bayesian 89% intervals; some effects anecdotal (BF 2.64 on direct variety).
agent_relevance: Exposure to a strong first example anchors output. Show the model one candidate at a time, not a favoured answer (G4, G5).

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2024) fixation displacement
finding: Qualitative: participants copied then tweaked AI images. Some fixation moved to the AI output, not the example, so the feature-count metric missed it. Some prompts (for example goddess, dragon) escaped the example.
numbers: 92 sketches in the AI condition; 10 made before any prompt were removed. 39 prompts held no words from the brief.
limits: Qualitative, small N. The metric counts shared features with the original example only.
agent_relevance: Fixation can shift to the latest sample. Measure similarity to all earlier attempts, not only the first.

source: Jansson and Smith (1991) design fixation, as described in Wadinambiarachchi et al. 2024
finding: Four experiments. Fixation group saw an example solution; control did not. Both produced similar numbers of designs, but fixation-group ideas were closer to the example. Later experiment: flexibility and originality were lower in the fixation group.
numbers: Four experiments; group sizes not given in the secondary text.
limits: Secondhand description; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Baseline human result that the LLM fixation papers replicate.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: GenAI shows its own design fixation. ChatGPT chair designs repeated themes and shared top words with Red Dot award designs (comfort, light, ergonomic, innovative, aesthetic).
numbers: Chair-structure keywords per 100 cases: Red Dot 208.57 vs ChatGPT 142.71. Midjourney vs Red Dot: global feature distance Red Dot 16.2509 (sd 3.2638) vs Midjourney 16.0503 (sd 4.3814); shape, colour, texture distances larger for Red Dot (p<0.01).
limits: Single product (chair); framework plus a small user study; no model version control beyond name.
agent_relevance: Model-side fixation is real: repeated themes across prompts. Use code-computed diversity checks before accepting a set of candidates.

source: Xu, Martelaro and McComb (2026) Supervising Ralph Wiggum: metacognitive co-regulation loop for engineering design
finding: LLM design agents fixate on existing paradigms. A second agent that monitors design progress (CRDAL) gave better battery-pack designs than a plain loop (RWL) or self-monitoring (SRL), at similar step counts.
numbers: 30 runs per system, up to 30 steps; ANOVA on capacity F(2,86)=21.606, p<0.001, partial eta^2=0.334; steps F(2,87)=0.031, p=0.97. Reported means: CRDAL 141.17 Ah, RWL 106.08 Ah, SRL 72.07 Ah. Text states SRL beat RWL (t(40.6)=3.715, p=0.001, d=0.956), which conflicts with those means.
limits: One problem, Gemini 3.1 Pro only, thinking level high, temperature 1.0. Internal mean/test inconsistency for SRL; one RWL run failed and was excluded.
agent_relevance: Supports an external monitor over self-monitoring (G1, G5). Treat the SRL result as uncertain until the inconsistency is resolved.

source: Miao et al. (2024) Diamond of Thought: design-thinking framework for LLMs in wearable design
finding: Alternating diverge and converge steps (double diamond) with retrieval from a database of 1,603 prototypes and 1,129 products. Compared with input-output and chain-of-thought prompting, and with human designers.
numbers: Ranking IO < CoT < DoT; DoT vs human designers not significantly different; six expert raters; GPT-4 API at temperature 0.7; four wearable design tasks.
limits: Small task set; raters were experts with embodied-cognition background; full test statistics not captured.
agent_relevance: A diverge/converge scaffold with retrieval beat plain chain of thought. Our states S0-S9 already alternate; the retrieval part is new.

source: Wadinambiarachchi et al. (2026, C&C) Reviving Reflection-in-Action
finding: Within-participants study of sketch, text and sketch-plus-tags prompting in an AI ideation tool. Sketch tended to raise fluency, but no credible difference in variety, originality or quality. Students preferred text.
numbers: 9 design students; 177 products (text 55, sketch 68, sketch-plus-tags 54); sketch had 95% probability of lower rating for expressing direction (b=-1.44, 89% CI [-3.35,-.03]).
limits: Preliminary, N=9, Bayesian 89% intervals, students not experts.
agent_relevance: Frictionless text prompting is preferred but may erode reflection. Our schema adds friction only on a signal (G1).

source: DesignerlyLoop (2025) forming design intent through curated reasoning
finding: Interviews with 8 experts and a 3-person design activity show LLM chat treats each prompt atomically and loses linked design decisions. A node-graph tool let users edit and link reasoning units. It scored higher than a baseline.
numbers: Controllability t(19)=3.65, p=.002; collaboration t(19)=2.80, p=.012; transparency p=.006; trust p<.001; 40 paired designs with self and expert ratings.
limits: Author list not recorded. Small samples; baseline was a plain chat. Designers used folders and tags to rebuild context by hand.
agent_relevance: Design decisions are linked and revisable. Keep explicit decision records and pass selected ones forward, as the tool does.

source: Canvil (2024) designerly adaptation for LLM-powered user experiences
finding: Uses Cross 1982 design codes: a two-way translation between abstract requirements and concrete designed objects. Interviews with 12 designers; tool lets design and model behaviour co-evolve on a canvas.
numbers: 12 formative interviews; the tool study sample was not read in detail.
limits: Authors not recorded here. Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Closest direct use of Cross 1982 with LLMs. Treat prompt and design as co-evolving, as in problem-solution co-evolution.

source: Rittel and Webber (1973) Dilemmas in a general theory of planning, Policy Sciences 4:155-169
finding: Recalled: ten properties of wicked problems, including no definitive formulation, no stopping rule, and solutions that are good or bad rather than true or false.
numbers: none
limits: Unverified. Cited in Cross 1982 reference list (opened).
agent_relevance: A stop rule has to be set from outside when no check exists.

source: Schon (1983) The Reflective Practitioner
finding: Recalled: designers converse with the situation, trying a move, reading what comes back, and reframing. Called reflection-in-action.
numbers: none
limits: Unverified; covered in the earlier subfield 02_reflection_in_action.
agent_relevance: Link to the revise-from-real-output rule G2.

source: Simon (1969) The Sciences of the Artificial
finding: Recalled: design is the science of how things ought to be; satisficing search in a space of alternatives. Cited in Cross 1982 reference list (opened).
numbers: none
limits: Unverified content.
agent_relevance: Satisficing matches a budgeted search with a stop rule.

source: Darke (1979) The primary generator and the design process, Design Studies 1(1):36-44
finding: Recalled: architects fix on a primary generator, an early guiding idea, then test it against constraints. Cited in the Cross 1982 reference list (opened).
numbers: Interview sample size not verified.
limits: Unverified content.
agent_relevance: Early conjecture followed by constraint test is a pattern for our attempt-and-check loop.

source: Cross (2004) Expertise in design: an overview, Design Studies 25(5)
finding: Cited in 2503.01631 for the claim that reframing is hard even for expert designers.
numbers: none
limits: Not opened; claim taken from the citing paper.
agent_relevance: Expert designers frame problems differently from novices. Expert-novice links go to the parallel subfield.

source: Cross, Naughton and Walker (1981) Design method and scientific method, Design Studies 2(4):195-201
finding: Cited in the Cross 1982 reference list (opened) as the contrast between design method and scientific method.
numbers: none
limits: Citation only.
agent_relevance: Background for why design is not a science-style search for truth.

source: Wikipedia: Design thinking (abductive reasoning section)
finding: Says designers infer possible solutions from available problem information, experience and non-deductive thinking, which it calls abductive reasoning.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary and thin.
agent_relevance: Abduction needs a check afterwards, so ties to G3 (test on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Cross 1982 reference list as reading map
finding: Reference list shows the sources Cross drew on: Ferguson 1977 (non-verbal thought in technology), Ryle 1949 (knowing how), Lakatos 1970, Alexander 1964 and 1979 (pattern language), March 1976 (logic of design), Rittel and Webber 1973.
numbers: none
limits: List only.
agent_relevance: Ryle's knowing-how vs knowing-that suggests design knowledge sits in practice and may not be fully writable as rules.

source: Wikipedia: Design thinking (problem framing section)
finding: Framing is described as reaching a particular framing of the problem that suggests a route to a solution.
numbers: none
limits: Secondary.
agent_relevance: Supports a reframe operator and links to the parallel Framing subfield.
